title: Use multi-line string to support multiple statements in R functions
description:
This PR proposes to use literal style multi-line string in YAML to support seamless formatting of R functions defined in the `knit` field and avoid possible confusions from indentation details.

Specifically, the current code example for customizing the knit button behavior works but does not work for any non-trivial R functions containing multiple statements. For example, let's add a `print(input)` call before the `rmarkdown::render` call. Using the current approach:

```yaml
knit: (function(input, ...) {
    print(input)
    rmarkdown::render(
      input,
      output_file = paste0(
      xfun::sans_ext(input), '-', Sys.Date(), '.html'
    ),
    envir = globalenv()
    )
  })
```

The function will be parsed as:

```text
[1] "(function(input, ...) { print(input) rmarkdown::render( input, output_file = paste0( xfun::sans_ext(input), '-', Sys.Date(), '.html' ), envir = globalenv() ) })"
```

This does not execute:

```text
Error: unexpected symbol in "(function(input, ...) { invisible(system(paste0('(function(input, ...) { print(input) rmarkdown::render( input, output_file = paste0( xfun::sans_ext(input), '-', Sys.Date(), '.html"
Execution halted
```

A workaround is adding `;` after the first statement, which is non-idiomatic.

Instead, if we write

```yaml
knit: |
  (function(input, ...) {
    print(input)
    rmarkdown::render(
      input,
      output_file = paste0(
      xfun::sans_ext(input), '-', Sys.Date(), '.html'
    ),
    envir = globalenv()
    )
  })
```

This will be parsed as:

```text
[1] "(function(input, ...) {\n  print(input)\n  rmarkdown::render(\n    input,\n    output_file = paste0(\n    xfun::sans_ext(input), '-', Sys.Date(), '.html'\n  ),\n  envir = globalenv()\n  )\n})"
```

which can be correctly executed.

In reality, users can write the R function separately, copy and paste it here, and simply add two spaces before each line.

title: Update trackdown now on cran
description:
Hi  @cderv,

Sorry for the time it took me to send this PR to update the old PR (#348) but it was a really busy month.

Now, the `trackdown` package is on CRAN ([link](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/trackdown/index.html)).  I have updated the information to install the package.
Note that I had to update the version of other packages as well because they are `trackdown` dependencies. In particular,

- cli 3.0
- gargle 1.2
- googledrive 2.0


Moreover, regarding the issue on `write_bib()` (knitr/issues/2028), the url is still missing from the reference because:

- although the package is now available on CRAN, the package is actually installed from the RSPM repository using `install.packages()`. This happens automatically probably for some default settings.  As a consequence, the following code is not evaluated

https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/d65b9239804163b693cbfa4b774980f3b7d1fecd/R/citation.R#L75-L80

- if I update `knitr` to the development version, the code below will process the first url but the url is still set in `note = ` and not in `url =` (as you already pointed out [link](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/2028#issuecomment-883259576)). The note field is not printed in the reference.

https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/d65b9239804163b693cbfa4b774980f3b7d1fecd/R/citation.R#L102-L105

In the PR I did not updated `knitr` to the development version to avoid installing through  GitHub. Let me know if you prefer I update it.

Thanks for your work!

title: Documentation of set-up process // building the HTML book
description:
Hi @cderv - Please find a first draft of the documentation for building the HTML book and let me know what you think. A few thoughts/questions as I went:

1. What are your thoughts on providing an `renv` option as in the STAT545 repo example? Initially, I was going to do this, but then I began to think: the local library would make the repo bigger and, unlike an analysis project, our usage of any of the dependent packages is fairly minimal. So, I'm not sure if the benefits of reproducibility here are worth it. Happy to do whichever you think is best. 

2. I called the file `SETUP.md` for now. I considered calling it `CONTRIBUTING.md` instead since that is more common; however, I don't know if we actually want to also use this file to talk about recommendations for others to engage with the project? So, for now, I just left it with a name to fully indicate it's strictly technical content. 

3. Related to 2, since these are instructions how to build the book, I also added text to recommend that PRs not include the built book. Generally, I find its slightly more convenient to have PRs not contain rendered HTML, but I know we can also deal with it on our end, so please let me know if you think that seems unfriendly to say. I'm happy to remove it.

4. I combed through the book, and if I'm not mistaken Asymptote is the only external software dependency. I notice in the language engine section that mostly the recipes (e.g. for python, SAS, and Stata) are not run. I am wondering if we should just screenshot the Asymptote output and not execute these chunks so we can run the book?

5. Given the Asymptote situation is unique, I simply added a chunk in that section to check for OS (since it seems not to work on Windows), installation of Asymptote, and the previously existing condition. I know you mentioned a function, and I like that idea but was not sure if the problems here were very generalizable. Let me know if you think differently or if there are other similar situations that I am missing.

Closes #291 

(By the way, apropos of nothing but this is the main way we interact -- I used your "cat engine to a temp file" recipe from the cookbook many times this week. If I recall, you originally wrote that based on a question I asked over in the `knitr` repo, so thanks again!)

description:
This PR contains my proofread of Chapter 7 (HTML).

- Highlight explicitly that the CSS selector for class `x` is `.x` (i.e. point out the leading dot since it's easy to miss in an example)
- Make more explicit that `.tabset` is applied to the "parent" of the headers that should be tabs (I often see people apply it to the headers which they want to become tabs)

I also made a few small structural changes:

- Moved the favicon recipe right after the `includes:` recipe since one uses the other

The other thing I noticed but did *not* change is that section 7.4 on scrollable blocks introduces code folding as an alternative. This is perhaps repetitive with 7.5 which is entirely about code folding. Do we want this content in both places?

title: Chapter 10 Proofreading
description:
This PR contains a handful of small changes for clarity/typos. I detailed each change in the commit message.

Additionally, I have a few issues I want to highlight for this chapter:

- In Section 10.2.2, the `strikeout = TRUE` option is not rendering in the PDF output, but it does work in the HTML output. I tried to dig in to why this is, and this is what I learned (all using the latest CRAN version of `kableExtra`).

  + This is not just true in `bookdown`, but the same thing happens when I copy that code chunk to a stand-alone Rmd and run it with `output: html_document` (which works) and `output: pdf_document` (which doesn't)
  + `strikeout` clearly can and should work in PDF, as indicated in [this GitHub issue](https://github.com/haozhu233/kableExtra/issues/99) and demonstrated in the package vignette ([output](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/kableExtra/vignettes/awesome_table_in_pdf.pdf) with example on p.10 and [source](https://github.com/haozhu233/kableExtra/blob/master/vignettes/awesome_table_in_pdf.Rmd))
  + The [LaTeX implementation](https://github.com/haozhu233/kableExtra/blob/9059e4bb189122fa30b456f5d2d6ca4b99f471bb/R/column_spec.R#L293) of the argument uses `sout` which is from the `ulem` LaTeX package
  + I was hopeful that declaring the LaTeX package dependency in the YAML header would work, but using either `header-includes` or `extra_dependencies` threw the error `LaTeX Error: Option clash for package ulem.` 
  + I'll admit I am quite a novice at LaTeX, so I thought I would check if any of this makes it obvious to you what is going on. Otherwise, I am happy to keep trying to debug. 

- When I added the references, I wasn't quite sure what to do with all the links in 10.3. Since the packages are not discussed in detail, these seemed potentially useful and like their purpose was greater than what the references replaced. However, currently there is a mix of references to GitHub and CRAN, although all the packages are on CRAN, and the section is very heavy on links relative to the rest of the book. Please let me know if you think I should strip them out.

- Currently, there's a completely blank page at the end of the chapter. We can check back on this after the final copy edits are in.

title: CSS reference draft
description:
This document is intended to close #229 by providing a translation between common markdown elements and CSS selectors. I struggled a bit here to think about the right content and formatting to include since it is a topic that can be infinitely broad and deep. For now, I only discuss the most common elements and most common cases and try to give the reader the tools to learn more on their own. I am very happy to try a different approach if anyone has other thoughts or preferences on the best content or structure. 

A few key questions:

- Where this should live? I started a new file because I was not sure if this should go in the HTML chapter or an appendix. It definitely seems too verbose to fit the style of the main text, but perhaps it is strange to have an appendix with only one topic? (Alternatively, I suppose the HTML hosting chapter could also "join" it in an appendix since that is also less of a recipe?)
- Would this section benefit by any diagrams or screenshots of the developer tools? My instinct is no, but let me know if you think it is worthwhile. 
- What is the best way to format the Common CSS Selectors section? Initially, I intended to make more of a table than write sentences. However, most all entries had enough exceptions and nuance that this became unmanageable. 
- In the issue, @yihui mentions a lack of understanding of the *cascading* part of style sheets. Should this document also have a section explain this? 

Thanks!

title: HTML output additions (favicon, hosting)
description:
This PR consists of two updates the the HTML output chapter.

## Favicon recipe ( closes #220 )

Provides basic instructions for adding a favicon to an RMarkdown website with the `includes:` argument. I tried to keep this part simple and short by showing the basic recipe and linking to outside web dev resources for more information on best practices or levels of complexity which are less useful for traditional RMarkdown usage.

## Hosting options ( closes #232 )

I followed @cderv 's outline in the issue fairly closely and mostly provided a list of common tools. I tried to avoid discussions of features that might change in the future. 

@cderv, I hope you will help keep me honest on my terminology for this part. I will admit I have fairly limited knowledge of the more technical side of web hosting (just my personal experience using GitHub Pages / Netlify). I double-checked most all of my terminology on the respective websites, but appreciate your eyes as well. I also had relatively little to say about GitLab Pages. There are many GitHub / GitLab feature comparisons online and since this is very likely to change over time it did not seem worth including. Let me know if you think that makes sense please. Thanks!

I have also linked to @yihui 's blog post about reasons to prefer Netlify over GitHub Pages. I hope that is alright! If so, should a blog post have a citation? I tried to find other examples of blog post references to see how they were handled, but I didn't find any.  Alternatively, instead of making this its own section, I could simply add a final sentence to the Netlify bullet that "The blogdown book makes a strong case for using Netlify".

description:
This PR is a first draft of the 'shared context' session we discussed via email. This is not yet ready 'for production', but I would appreciate any feedback on the scope of the content included, writing style, or any other direction you wish to provide. I'm happy to make any sort of changes and explore other approaches.

Here are a few questions that I debated while writing, and I would appreciate any advice you have:

- Is this the right content? 
  + I think my slow realization of all of these topics has definitely helped me navigate RMarkdown but I obviously don't want to overfit to my own experience.
- Is the level of explanation appropriate? 
  + Since our goal is to establish a shared context, I tend towards overexplaining instead of underexplaining and, to some extent, explaining helpful (I hope!) heuristics versus the full technical mechanisms. This ultimately targets the less experienced readers. 
  + On one hand, this hopefully helps level the playing field for them, but on the other hand, I don't want to give more experienced readers a bad first impression of the book! 
- Is the length too long for the amount of content?
- Am I too heavy on cross-references to sections that readers will not have seen yet? 
  + My hope is to make a 'marketing pitch' and grow excitement for the future chapters by teasing what is to come, but perhaps it is confusing to reference future material.
- Should the writing style be more formal or casual? I also know that my writing tends to be a bit more verbose / conversational. I can make this more direct if we prefer.
- Of course, also open to other feedback or directions!

After we resolve any content issues, below are some notes on technical things that I would need to fix before this PR were ready to merge:

- Currently, the 'What happens when we render?' section is blank. I'm wondering if it would be appropriate to pull 2.1 up into this context piece. (Unless this chapter should be appendix material, at which point I can make a reference to 2.1)
- A few sections I would like to cross-reference do not have named headers. May I add those to the other sections? Alternatively, I can verbally reference concepts without formally cross-referencing.
- I made a few mockup `nomnoml` figures to help illustrate what I was talking about. Please let me know if I should remove these (I get the sense some publishers prefer fewer figures?) or rewrite in a different format (other package and/or replace with static image) to avoid the `nomnoml` dependency. This was just an easy way to quickly illustrate what I was picturing.
- The file needs to be renamed and linked to the book

Best,

Emily

title: use lineNumbers in revealjs and automate lineNumbers of chunks
description:
`revealjs::revealjs_presentation` by default hides line numbers.
So I showed a small CSS to show them.

Also, I described how to automatically add line numbers with chunks.
I think most users interested in this topic need line numbers to all chunks.
Thus I consider the automation is worth reading for such users.

Here is a reproducible Rmd.

````
---
output:
  html_document:
    highlight: pygments
---

```{r, include=FALSE}
# A function to generate hook functions
numberLines <- function(code = c("source", "output", "warning", "error")) {
  .code <- match.arg(code)
  .attr <- paste0("attr.", code)

  function(options) {
    if (.code %in% options$numberLines) {
      options[[.attr]] <- c(options[[.attr]], ".numberLines")
    }
    options
  }
}

# Set hooks
knitr::opts_hooks$set(
  attr.source = numberLines("source"),
  attr.output = numberLines("output"),
  attr.warning = numberLines("warning"),
  attr.error = numberLines("error")
)

# Fire hooks by fix attr.* to a blank string (or any but `NULL`)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  attr.source = "",
  attr.output = "",
  attr.warning = "",
  attr.error = "",
  numberLines = c("source", "output", "warning", "error")
)
```


# With line numbers

```{r}
1
warning("BOO")
```


# Without line numbers

```{r, numberLines=NULL}
1
```
````

title: Font color for HTML output: font tag is obsolete
description:
You are doing an amazing work!

Since the goal of the book is to provide up-to-date solutions, I think the tip provided to modify font color for HTML output should be updated because the `<font>` tag is obsolete (see https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/font).

Even if it is still supported by browsers, it is highly recommended to not use this tag.

Here is a small proposal to use CSS instead of the `<font>` tag.

title: Review on table part
description:
Hi, This is a PR that act as reviews for #161 As you do not work with PR yourself, it is not easy to comment in the doc directly, so I test this process. You can consider each commit as a remark and a suggestion for improvement. With this PR we have a room for discussion, and you'll then have the opportunity to revert a commit to not accept a remark: ```bash # revert a commit by comiting the inverse of the commit git revert 5508d78d # revert a commit by staging the reverting change but with opportunity to adjust git revert -n 5508d78d ``` You can also cherry pick what is interesting. We will see if this is working as a process or not. ### In this review #### Table of argument The table of argument is nice, particularly to show unknown arguments hidden in `knitr:::kable_*` function. Instead of creating manually the table, we can do programmatically to get * all the args * the default value ``` r library(magrittr) filter_out <- c("x", "...") to_table <- function(args, HTML = FALSE, Latex = FALSE, Markdown = FALSE) { tibble::tibble( Argument = names(args), Description = NA, HTML = HTML, Latex = Latex, Markdown = Markdown, Default = vapply(args, rlang::as_label, FUN.VALUE = "") ) } extract_args <- function(fun) { args <- rlang::fn_fmls(fun) args <- args[setdiff(names(args), filter_out)] } # get all args from default function all_args <- to_table(extract_args(knitr::kable), HTML = TRUE, Latex = TRUE, Markdown = TRUE) # get args from specific html function html_args <- to_table(extract_args(knitr:::kable_html), HTML = TRUE) html_args <- html_args[!html_args$Argument %in% all_args$Argument,] # get args from specific latex function latex_args <- to_table(extract_args(knitr:::kable_latex), Latex = TRUE) latex_args <- latex_args[!latex_args$Argument %in% all_args$Argument,] # get args from specific markdown function markdown_args <- to_table(extract_args(knitr:::kable_markdown), Markdown = TRUE) markdown_args <- markdown_args[!markdown_args$Argument %in% all_args$Argument,] # format table rbind(all_args, html_args, latex_args, markdown_args) %>% knitr::kable(caption = "Possible arguments for the kable function") ```

description: When building the book, there was some warnings about knitr engines that were not know and then should be set.
